{
  "hook": "1,350 m up the eastern shoulder of Tupungato, Atamisque’s Chardonnay grows on free-draining, calcareous sand left by old Andes alluvial fans. That altitude and limestone-starved soil give you stone-fruit precision framed by a salty snap you rarely taste in New-World Chardonnay at this price.",
  "wine_summary": "Atamisque was the first property in Valle de Tupungato to plant Burgundian clones at 1,200-1,400 m, and it still works those blocks for tension rather than weight. The 2018 carries 13.5% alcohol, partial malolactic, and 30% new Frenche oak, translating the vineyard’s cool diurnal swing into white-peach flesh and a chalk-dust finish that outruns most $30 California bottles. Seven Berliner golds in ten years tell you the judges keep noticing; the real story is that the estate’s irrigation water melts straight off granite peaks, so berries stay tiny and phenolics ripe without flab.",
  "terroir_expression": "Alluvial sands mixed with limestone pebbles drain winter snowmelt fast, forcing roots to dive 3 m for water stored in fractured granite below. That stress limits berry size, thickens skins, and pumps malic acid into the pulp—think white nectarine, not mango. Night temperatures routinely drop 16°C, locking the acid in while the high-UV sun burnishes phenolics, so you get nectarine flesh plus a citrus-oil snap that reads like Puligny on a budget.",
  "vinification_summary": "Hand-picked at 22.5°Brix, whole-cluster pressed, then 30% ferments in 300-liter new Névers barrels with bâtonnage every two weeks for four months. Partial (about 40%) malolactic softens the sharp malic edge to yogurt-cream lactic, while the remaining malic acid keeps the finish saline; the rest ages in stainless on fine lees to preserve the high-altitude cut.",
  "food_pairing": [
    "Nashville hot chicken—the wine’s salty acid cools spicy capsaicin while its peachy fruit mirrors the sweet brine.",
    "Trout gravlox with dill crème fraîche: the citrus pith notes slice through oily fish, partial ML matches the cream.",
    "Veal chop with morel cream sauce: moderate body and hazelnut oak echo the browned butter, acidity scours the morelores’ earth.",
    "Aged Comté (18 months): high-altitude acidity tackles crystalline tyrosine, stone fruit plays off nutty paste.",
    "Sushi omakase—especially kohada or ch scallop: oceanic salinity mirrors soy/mirin, gentle oak doesn’t crush delicate raw fish."
  ],
  "comparable_wines": [
    "Catena Alta Chardonnay — same altitude band but more new oak and full ML, giving broader, toastier palate at +$15.",
    "Portillo Bodega Chardonnay — also Tupungato, sand over granite, yet stainless only and zero ML, sharper but less texture for -$8.",
    "Bourgogne Blanc ‘Côte d’Or’ (e.g., Ropiteau) — similar limestone cut and peach fruit, but 1er cru pricing starts 30% higher for equivalent ripeness."
  ],
  "style_profile": "Medium-bodied dry white with bright stone-fruit core and salty limestone snap",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink 2018-2024 to catch the primary peach/hazelnut drive; after five years the modest ML yields more hazelnut but fruit at the cost of the high-toned fruit. Keep at 12°C, 70% humidity—no need to splurge on Champagne storage.",
  "value_assessment": "Expect to pay USD 22-26 in most U.S. markets. At that tag it undercuts entry-level Sonoma Coast Chardonnay by $7 and outruns most $30 Mâcon for mineral tension. The only real peer near $25 is Leyda Reserve from Chile, but Leyda carries more overt pineapple; for limestone snap under thirty bucks, this is currently the sharpest knife in the bin.",
  "market_position": "You’ll spot it by-the-glass at Buenos Aires parrillas and on hip NYC lists that need a food-friendly white under sixty dollars retail markup. Not a collector bottle—production sits around 8,000 cases—so it moves through retail stacks aimed at week-night Burgundy drinkers priced out of 2020 Côte d’Or.",
  "insider_take": "Ignore the gold medals; the real signal is altitude plus limestone-poor soil—two variables New-World Chardonnay rarely combines this cheap. Skip it if you need buttery movie-popcorn opulence; buy a case if you want Puligny tension at Happy Hour money.",

parsed.hook: 1,350 m up the eastern shoulder of Tupungato, Atamisque’s Chardonnay grows on free-draining, calcareous sand left by old Andes alluvial fans. That altitude and limestone-starved soil give you stone-fruit precision framed by a salty snap you rarely taste in New-World Chardonnay at this price.
parsed.wine_summary: Atamisque was the first property in Valle de Tupungato to plant Burgundian clones at 1,200-1,400 m, and it still works those blocks for tension rather than weight. The 2018 carries 13.5% alcohol, partial malolactic, and 30% new Frenche oak, translating the vineyard’s cool diurnal swing into white-peach flesh and a chalk-dust finish that outruns most $30 California bottles. Seven Berliner golds in ten years tell you the judges keep noticing; the real story is that the estate’s irrigation water melts straight off granite peaks, so berries stay tiny and phenolics ripe without flab.
parsed.terroir_expression: Alluvial sands mixed with limestone pebbles drain winter snowmelt fast, forcing roots to dive 3 m for water stored in fractured granite below. That stress limits berry size, thickens skins, and pumps malic acid into the pulp—think white nectarine, not mango. Night temperatures routinely drop 16°C, locking the acid in while the high-UV sun burnishes phenolics, so you get nectarine flesh plus a citrus-oil snap that reads like Puligny on a budget.
parsed.vinification_summary: Hand-picked at 22.5°Brix, whole-cluster pressed, then 30% ferments in 300-liter new Névers barrels with bâtonnage every two weeks for four months. Partial (about 40%) malolactic softens the sharp malic edge to yogurt-cream lactic, while the remaining malic acid keeps the finish saline; the rest ages in stainless on fine lees to preserve the high-altitude cut.
food_pairing: Nashville hot chicken—the wine’s salty acid cools spicy capsaicin while its peachy fruit mirrors the sweet brine.
Trout gravlox with dill crème fraîche: the citrus pith notes slice through oily fish, partial ML matches the cream.
Veal chop with morel cream sauce: moderate body and hazelnut oak echo the browned butter, acidity scours the morelores’ earth.
Aged Comté (18 months): high-altitude acidity tackles crystalline tyrosine, stone fruit plays off nutty paste.
Sushi omakase—especially kohada or ch scallop: oceanic salinity mirrors soy/mirin, gentle oak doesn’t crush delicate raw fish.
comparable_wines: Catena Alta Chardonnay — same altitude band but more new oak and full ML, giving broader, toastier palate at +$15.
Portillo Bodega Chardonnay — also Tupungato, sand over granite, yet stainless only and zero ML, sharper but less texture for -$8.
Bourgogne Blanc ‘Côte d’Or’ (e.g., Ropiteau) — similar limestone cut and peach fruit, but 1er cru pricing starts 30% higher for equivalent ripeness.

parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink 2018-2024 to catch the primary peach/hazelnut drive; after five years the modest ML yields more hazelnut but fruit at the cost of the high-toned fruit. Keep at 12°C, 70% humidity—no need to splurge on Champagne storage.
parsed.value_assessment: Expect to pay USD 22-26 in most U.S. markets. At that tag it undercuts entry-level Sonoma Coast Chardonnay by $7 and outruns most $30 Mâcon for mineral tension. The only real peer near $25 is Leyda Reserve from Chile, but Leyda carries more overt pineapple; for limestone snap under thirty bucks, this is currently the sharpest knife in the bin.

Not a collector bottle—production sits around 8,000 cases—so it moves through retail stacks aimed at week-night Burgundy drinkers priced out of 2020 Côte d’Or.
parsed.insider_take: Ignore the gold medals; the real signal is altitude plus limestone-poor soil—two variables New-World Chardonnay rarely combines this cheap. Skip it if you need buttery movie-popcorn opulence; buy a case if you want Puligny tension at Happy Hour money.
